urgent.heading: Seek medical advice for a new concern
paragraphs: Do not assume a new injury or symptom is explained by hypermobility. A suspected dislocation, significant injury or new concerning symptoms need appropriate medical assessment.
For a severe or life-threatening emergency, call 000. If you are unsure about a concerning symptom, seek medical advice.

pattern.heading: Flexibility alone does not mean a disorder
pattern.intro: Some people have joints that move beyond the usual range without symptoms. Others have pain or movement concerns that affect their day.

items.title: Flexibility without symptoms
items.copy: Joint hypermobility can be a physical trait. Being flexible on its own does not establish HSD or hEDS.

items.title: Pain or a feeling of instability
items.copy: Describe what happens and which movements are difficult. These concerns deserve assessment rather than an assumption about their cause.

items.title: Activity that takes more effort
items.copy: Tell your clinician about fatigue or other health concerns as well as joint symptoms. Coexisting conditions can change what support is appropriate.

items.title: Questions about a diagnosis
items.copy: A screening score cannot provide the whole answer. Your GP or specialist can help you seek appropriate diagnostic assessment.

explainer.heading: Hypermobility, HSD and hEDS
paragraphs: Joint hypermobility describes a greater range of movement at one or more joints. Hypermobility spectrum disorders (HSD) involve symptomatic hypermobility after other explanations are considered. Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) has clinical diagnostic criteria.

HSD is not simply a milder version of hEDS. Either can affect daily life and need support. Diagnosis considers history, examination and other possible explanations; it cannot be made from flexibility or a checklist alone.

Alpha can assess movement and provide musculoskeletal support. We do not formally diagnose hEDS or HSD. Discuss diagnostic questions with your GP or specialist; appropriate referral can be considered.

focus.heading: Work with your current tolerance
paragraphs: Alpha’s hypermobility service is led clinically by Dr Ashton Wilson, an osteopath. At our Newport clinic, you can discuss joint symptoms and the activities you want support with. Ask reception about suitable practitioners and appointment options.

Strengthening and movement-control work can be considered individually. The exercise, range and amount of work need to suit your circumstances. Tell the clinician how you respond, including effects after an appointment.

Coexisting conditions matter. If you have ME/CFS or symptoms that worsen after exertion, general exercise progression may be inappropriate. Seek advice from your medical or specialist team; you should not be encouraged to push through those symptoms.

process.heading: Build the plan around your daily activities

steps.title: Describe your experience
steps.copy: Talk about joint symptoms, health history and what you would like support with.

steps.title: Share your medical context
steps.copy: Bring up diagnosed conditions, relevant investigations and advice from other treating professionals.

steps.title: Consider movement
steps.copy: The clinician discusses appropriate assessment and how your symptoms affect movement.

steps.title: Discuss suitable options
steps.copy: Ask about movement support, exercise or other musculoskeletal care, including its limits and alternatives.

steps.title: Review how you respond
steps.copy: Describe how you respond to the plan, including any delayed worsening. Further changes depend on that response.

steps.title: Keep care connected
steps.copy: Discuss communication with your GP or another treating professional where useful and with your consent.

note.heading: The answer depends on the joint and the person
paragraphs: A blanket instruction never to stretch is not useful for everyone with hypermobility. Some tight muscles may need careful stretching; an already mobile joint may need a different approach.
The Ehlers-Danlos Society describes individual strengthening and movement-control support. Discuss exercise selection with a clinician who can consider your symptoms and other health needs.

faqs.question: Does being flexible mean I have hEDS?
faqs.answer: No. Joint hypermobility can occur without a disorder. hEDS has clinical diagnostic criteria and requires assessment of more than flexibility. Discuss diagnostic concerns with your GP or specialist.

faqs.question: Can Alpha diagnose HSD or hEDS?
faqs.answer: No. Alpha can assess movement and offer musculoskeletal support, but does not formally diagnose hEDS or HSD. Your GP or specialist can help you seek appropriate diagnostic assessment.

faqs.question: Is HSD a milder form of hEDS?
faqs.answer: No. They are distinct diagnostic categories. The name alone does not tell you how much someone’s symptoms affect daily life.

faqs.question: Should I avoid all stretching?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Some tight muscles may benefit from careful stretching, and already mobile joints may need other approaches. Ask for advice that considers the joint, symptoms and your individual circumstances.

faqs.question: Should I keep increasing my exercise?
faqs.answer: Exercise needs to be considered around your tolerance and other health conditions. Do not assume fixed increases suit you. If you have ME/CFS or worsening after exertion, seek medical or specialist guidance rather than pushing through.

faqs.question: Can I have an online appointment?
faqs.answer: Alpha offers telehealth for hypermobility support. Contact reception to confirm current availability, suitability and what the appointment can cover.

faqs.question: Can I claim a rebate?
faqs.answer: Funding depends on the practitioner, service and your cover or eligibility. Confirm requirements and fees with reception and your insurer before attending.
